text: Last lesson of Chapter Five. Dynamic SQL means building a SQL statement as a string at runtime and running it — useful when you don't know the table name or query shape until the code is actually executing. But that power comes with a real security rule that applies on every single platform here: if you build that string by pasting raw user input straight into it, you've opened the door to SQL injection.

T-SQL's safer path is covered in depth elsewhere in this catalog, but here's the shape. Declare at sql n varchar max equals select star from production dot product where product id equals at id, exec sp underscore executesql at sql, n at id int, at id equals seven oh seven. That's a real bind variable, at id, filled in separately — never concatenated into the string itself. Exec parentheses alone has no parameter support at all, which is why sp underscore executesql is the better choice.

PL/SQL does this in one single statement. V underscore sql varchar2 equals select list price from products where product id equals colon id, execute immediate v underscore sql into v underscore price using v underscore id. Colon id is the named bind variable placeholder, and using fills it in — one statement, start to finish.

MySQL is structurally different here, and it's worth remembering clearly. Set at product id equals seven oh seven, prepare stmt from select list price from products where product id equals question mark, execute stmt using at product id, deallocate prepare stmt. That's three separate statements, not one — prepare compiles and names it, execute runs it with your bind value filling in the question mark, and deallocate prepare releases it when you're done.

PostgreSQL's PL slash pgsql goes back to one statement, much like Oracle. Execute, select list price from products where product id equals dollar one, into v underscore price using v underscore id. Dollar one is a positional placeholder, filled by using — one statement, close in shape to PL/SQL's execute immediate, just with a different placeholder style.

Whichever platform you're on — T-SQL, PL/SQL, MySQL, or Postgres — the rule never changes: bind variables for user input, always, never string concatenation. That closes out Chapter Five. Next, Chapter Six goes deep into Oracle's own procedural language, starting with the basic shape of a PL/SQL block — declare, begin, exception, end. See you there.
